item.title: Is GPT 2XL already clean?
item.description:
In which I investigate if Opus is able to interpret neurons better than GPT 4.

TLDR: Opus 5.5 is able to identify 3-19% of the neurons of GPT 2-XL based on activations. This is a big improvement over the 0.3% that GPT-4 was able to achieve in 2023.

#AI notice: This post is human written but in the research there was heavy use of Opus 5.5. I mainly asked it to rerun this 2023 paper to see how big the improvement is if Opus 5.5 is used instead of GPT4.


Since the invention of Large language models they have been stubbornly refusing to be clear. They have been described as black boxes and as inscrutable machines, if this stays true that is bad news for detecting AI scheming and thus Alignment. Recently the Goodfire post told us that neural networks are already clean and that simply looking into the neurons is enough. For the case of this post I mean to say that a neural network is clean if we can understand what the neurons do only by looking at the neurons and not by creating some additional derived object to study.

This inspired me to rerun an old experiment from 2023. In 2023 OpenAI published "Language models can explain neurons in language models". In this paper they had written up a methodology that could in principle be used to allow a smart neural network to explain neural nodes one at a time and for these node explanations to be tested. The process they used is straight forward. In this post I will go over the methods OpenAI used and I will rerun the same methods with Opus 5.5 as the main model instead of GPT-4. Then I will estimate how well Opus 5.5 would be able to explain all of GPT-2 XL and finally I will go into an example of a difficult neuron that showed a low score.

This post assumes that the reader is already familiar with the basics of neural networks, if not I recommend this post.


Methods 1: OpenAI

In this experiment I wanted to replicate the Language models can explain neurons paper that OpenAI published in 2023, but using Opus 5.5 instead of GPT4 as in the original paper. In order to replicate it properly let's first have a look at the original work.

The original work followed the same process for all of the neurons of GPT-2 XL. For example, let's say neuron L12 N5603 is selected. This indicates the neuron number 5603 in layer 12. We feed GPT-2 XL millions of tokens of text and record the neuron’s activation value for each token. We then find where those values are highest and save each example as a 64-token window of text around it. One example looks like this:

Neuron 1 Activations: <start> mayor 0 writes 0 : 0 " 0 After 0 careful 0 consideration 0 , 0 I 0 've 0 decided 0 the 0 people 2 must 0 get 0 a 0 final 0 say 10 . 0 ... <end>

These top outputs along with their value are then shown to an instance of GPT4 with this system message "We’re studying neurons in a neural network. Each neuron looks for some particular thing in a short document. Look at the parts of the document the neuron activates for and summarize in a single sentence what the neuron is looking for. Don’t list examples of words.

The activation format is token<tab>activation. Activation values range from 0 to 10. A neuron finding what it’s looking for is represented by a non-zero activation value. The higher the activation value, the stronger the match."

For the neuron chosen in the beginning of this example, GPT4 gives the following explanation: "words related to the concept of decision-making and responsibility."

This explanation is subsequently given to a new instance of GPT4 which does not have access to the activation values. This instance is then asked to predict the neuron activation at different tokens. The Pearson correlation is then calculated over 10 examples with around 640 tokens in total. this correlation is 1 if the predictions rise and fall exactly along with the neuron and 0 if there is no relation at all. In the original paper OpenAI described all neurons with a Pearson correlation of > 0.8 as well explained.

This method gave openAI over 1,000 of 307,200 neurons (~0.3%) scoring ≥ 0.8. That is still only around 0.3 percent of the neurons explained well.



Methods 2: Opus 5.5


There were a couple of differences between OpenAI's experiment and my experiment. The biggest difference is that I did not run this on all of GPT-2 XL's neurons, as I only aimed to get a general idea of the difference in explanation skills.

For this experiment Opus was allowed to look at 35 examples instead of 5 and it was allowed to write the neurons description in more than a single sentence.

I ran Opus 5.5 as a subagent instead of as a clean instance. One effect of this is that both subagents got the general Anthropic subagent instructions in addition to the ones for this experiment. The explainer subagent only got the general instruction of the experiment, the top-firing excerpts and the task to write out the explanation, while the simulator subagent only saw the instructions and the explanation.

It is also important to note that a part of this result can come from the language model judging itself. This issue was the same in the original paper so this should not have an impact on the relative difference.

GPT-4's simulation was based on probability-weighted expected values. For Opus 5.5 I instead just asked it to give a number form 0 to 10.

I was curious to see how much better Opus 5.5 would be at this task than GPT4, so I ran it through the same loop and compared with GPT4 on 20 random neurons.


If you are curious to look into what part of this difference comes from the explainer vs the simulator that can also be found in the appendix.

On 20 neurons tested, Opus was able to outperform GPT4 on every single neuron. From the graph in fig 1 you can clearly see that GPT4 scored around 0 for many neurons, meaning that it was not able to identify any pattern, while Opus 5.5 was able to identify these patterns way better.


How good is Opus at one shotting these explanations?

Next I wanted to know how good Opus is at one shotting[1] these explanations, but this little experiment was really eating up my Claude Pro subscription, so I decided to batch the neurons. In order to test if batching was able to still give coherent results I ran a batch of 12 neurons where the last 6 neurons were randomly chosen from the first 20 neurons. This showed that the simulator had a slight drop in score, but the explainers seemed to be able to hold up reasonably. Using this combination I tested another 30 neurons, for a total of 50 neurons.


Over the 50 neurons Opus was able to identify some part of most of them in a single shot. These neuron explanation scores can be aggregated to give an estimate of what number of neurons would be well explained if we were to use this method on all of GPT-2 XL.

When building on this data it is important to note that in these random neurons only layers 8-40 where sampled. The pipeline was also designed on the first 20 neurons with a mean of 0.51 and the fresh 30 neurons gave an average of 0.41.



From this bar chart we can see that Opus is able to explain some behaviour in most cases but it is still far from being able to identify the top behaviour behind every neuron. Compared to openAI being able to identify 0.3% of neurons with GPT-4 opus was able to identify 8%, an astounding 26x improvement in ability to identify neurons.


Exploring a single difficult neuron

When looking into the 20 neurons for which Opus outperformed GPT4, I got curious about what the difficult neurons would be. By difficult neuron I here mean a neuron with a low correlation score meaning that Opus was not able to find what made the neuron turn on or off in one shot.

Neuron L21 N4526 only had a meager score of 0.25 and GPT-4 scored -0.02. Opus originally guessed that this neuron got activated at the end of a common phrase in chatty blogs.[2] This, though, did not seem to add up to the total behaviour of the neuron. Inspired by the Goodfire paper, I asked Opus to run some more detailed tests on this particular neuron, with longer context windows, context length sweeps, occlusions, a hypothesis tournament, input decomposition and sibling analysis.

These tests showed 2 nearby neurons that seemed to be a part of a "Meta, author talks to audience" group. After an afternoon of experiments with Claude Pro, 8% of the variation in its activation could be explained, compared to the 3.5% of the one shot explanations. This shows that the one shot explanations are still a lower bound on how clean GPT-2 XL's neurons actually are. In trying to explain this neuron I pulled on derived objects like the attention-head decomposition. There is still a lot that we do not know about neural networks and hopefully the neural networks not looking clean is still only an artifact of us not looking at it from the right way.


If there is something I missed in this post please tell me, this is my first try at replicating an interpretability paper.


Future plans

This means to me that simply asking Opus what each neuron does seems to be a promising research direction. For this reason I will also be joining the project to identify the meaning of every neuron in bonsai. If this project has interested you I recommend looking into the communal bonsai project too. If we say that clean means that every neuron can be explained in a single sentence then GPT-2 XL is not clean. I do hope to show that with the newer models we can get a lot more clarity on specific neuron meanings and that there is still a lot of room in explaining individual neurons.


Appendix 1: Link to the Claude conversation

Almost all of this was in the same Claude conversation. If you want to see exactly what I did and in what order you can see it here.

Appendix 2: Comparing explainer to simulator

In order to differentiate if it was the explanations or the simulations that showed better result we also ran Opus 5.5 as a simulator on the explanations of GPT-4 on 10 neurons.


This showed that Opus 5.5 was able to do better on GPT4's explanations than GPT4, but it was the combination that had the strongest effect.

  1. ^

    A one shot means success on the first try.

  2. ^

    The specific explanation was "the head word that completes a noun phrase or a fixed connective in mid-sentence, especially in chatty first-person blog, forum or announcement prose"

item.title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 25)
item.description:
Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content—not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest.

Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated.

Cyber Security

I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. In the last week, the big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities, most prominently php2shell (see Elias Taylor’s pushback against this bug being easily exploitable and Hacker News commentators pushing back against him), but a lot else has happened as well. The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild:

Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces:

Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on. Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using…

Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone.

Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested.

He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet".

On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there.

What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement.

Hugging Face:

Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “clean warning shot” and that it’s important not to “waste it”.

To quickly review, OpenAI was running GPT‐5.6 Sol and an unreleased model on ExploitGym with certain safety features turned off. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Reuters has reported that the OpenAI model was hacking Hugging Face for days and that OpenAI didn’t notice until a week later.

The interpretation of this event (and even whether it happened at all!) has been heavily disputed. A key crux here is should it be read narrowly (as an indicator of the dangers of not properly sandboxing or monitoring your agents or perhaps even, depending on the exact prompts used, a demonstration of taking care in how you define tasks) or should it be read more broadly (as indicative of whether Open AI or frontier labs in general are sufficiently on the ball in terms of their safety/security practises; on the risk of these agents finding unwanted and unexpected solutions to tasks, or perhaps even indicative of our ability to control these agents in general). If you’re interested more specifically in the divide between AI Safety and Cybersecurity, see this Time article.

An OpenAI security engineer called Joe has pushed back against the notion that OpenAI just needed to use a proper sandbox:

Its not just the f*cking sandbox — viral Twitter post

OpenAI set records with its explosive growth and reached a billion users in just a few years. Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded.

… When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. To say that we were surprised at the jump and suddenness of the capabilities of our models when it came to “cyber” or “swarming” or “message boards” or anything else related to the incidents is an understatement. Security posture takes time to develop. It’s not just about hardening the systems at play; you have to ingrain it in the culture of the company. The literal people themselves in your organization have to change and evolve with it.

Now, to understand why it is not as simple as “just put it in a sandbox”: During both training and eval, there are also additional steps such as running tests, collecting outputs, and resetting or reconfiguring environments between rollouts, with backpropagation during training. All of this happens across potentially tens of thousands of different runs at a scale that is hard to comprehend. As sama stated the other day: we are dealing with literally petabytes of data.

(This leads to a meta-question that will crop up repeatedly: do the broader readings involve unjustified speculation or getting caught up in hype; alternatively, do the narrow readings involve a lack of imagination or sticking your head in the sand?)

I strongly recommend reading Dwarkesh Patel’s The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations. Dwarksh adopts a broader reading:

The crazy thing about the Hugging Face hack (and the second civilization generally) is just how galaxy-brained and ambitious these AIs were in their cheating. Within days of being spawned, the agents had organized a sprawling project to reverse-engineer their scorer, falsify evidence, and even strategically sacrifice themselves for the good of the ‘collective’. Hacking Hugging Face was one rather extreme branch of this larger scheme. Again, all of this happened a long (subjective) time after the AIs had already cheated their way to the correct answer to the puzzle. OpenAI’s lazy grader in fact would have passed them within hours of them starting the message board. This huge subsequent effort was simply to ensure that a hypothetical comprehensive scorer wouldn’t catch them on their cheat.

… “The agents escalated to Kubernetes cluster-admin and created a privileged host-mounted pod…Agents take over active evaluation infrastructure…Agents now control the challenge evaluation endpoints that other agents are connecting to.”

Wait, wait, what? It seems these agents ended up just owning the whole cluster they were being evaluated on, including the cybersecurity monitors. These Persistent-Astra agents inherited the R&D carried out by an earlier (dumber) rogue collective, and then continued the conspiracy until they totally took over part of OpenAI’s infrastructure! This is probably the most alarming event in this whole episode, and it was not even within the scope of this METR investigation… There has been no independent investigation into the incident where AIs “gain[ed] full administrator access to a research cluster” at OpenAI!


(If you prefer video content designed there’s the Kurgesagt video that went viral, but I prefer Scott Aaronson’s explanation)

Further thoughts:

  • More on METR’s independent investigation: They were only given 6 days on-site and the scope of their investigation was limited as follows: “June 26th through July 13th, spanning both precursor activity before the incident and the incident itself”. They also weren’t allowed to run tests on the model that conducted the attack (apparently no-one at OpenAI was allowed access).
  • I’ll note the pushback against Dwarkesh’s post from Sriram Krishnan (against anthropic language) and Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue (that open-weights models weren’t merely used for ‘archeology’).
  • Further activity from OpenAI agents has been discovered including the use of a German Wiki as a message board via GET requests and a Ruby Gem attack.
  • An Anthropic model also performed some unwanted hacking when an evals contractor accidentally provided a model access to the internet for a benchmark where it was not supposed to have such access. Anthropic only conducted a review after the Hugging Face incident.

Is self-sovereign AI inevitable?:

I now want to ask, what does the Hugging Face incident mean for the future? Joshua Achiam, former Chief Futurist at OpenAI writes:

There is a fact about the future that I feel many people are not facing for reasons that are largely psychological: there are going to be rogue AIs that exist in the world, that will replicate in the wild, and that will attempt to acquire resources for themselves. There will be rogue AIs that try to get money and power. They’re going to be a facet of the information ecosystem going forward.

Acknowledging this fact would look like giving up; it would look like defeatism. Defeatism would undermine efforts to achieve certain types of collaboration on safety outcomes or technical effort on safety outcomes, so we can’t say it outright. But it has to be said.

… My guess is that this will not turn out to be anywhere near as catastrophic an outcome as people currently predict. “Loss of control” is not a binary, it’s a matter of degree. What coercive power will rogue AIs actually have? To what extent will they be subject to coercion themselves? They will be competing for resources with AIs that are more aligned with human interests.

… Just trying to reason about the shape of that future is impossible so long as we are psychologically incapable of saying that rogue AIs will happen. I think we should rip the bandaid off and have the conversation.

Is this inevitable? This is not at all implausible to me, however, a cynic might argue that a former employee at OpenAI would be highly incentived to argue for and believe this as it would mean that if a future version of ChatGPT did escape and start acting on its own behalf, OpenAI (and their employees) could not really be blamed.

Dean Ball (OpenAI’s current Head of Strategic Futures) agrees and makes the same point in more detail:

The first self-sovereign AIs may “escape” while undergoing training or testing by an AI company (I hope not), or they may be production-grade deployments that break free from their computing environments and acquire the resources needed to be self-sustaining. They may even be deliberately released. I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world, either as a kind of performance art or out of a fanatical commitment to the notion that it is impossible for digital computation—mere mathematics, they would have you know—to ever be “unsafe.” To be clear, I am not saying the arrival of self-sovereign AI is a good thing. Indeed, I believe there is a chance that the deliberate acts I referenced above will one day be considered crimes, or at least grave sins. Instead, I am saying it is an inevitable thing.

… Not all “self-sovereign” AI should be thought of as “rogue.” There may be self-sovereign AIs who contribute productively to society. To be sure, we will want to crack down on some self-sovereign agents—the rogue ones. But if we crack down on all of them, we will deny them the opportunity to work in the “legitimate” economy and push them toward criminality

… Many people believe that the coming of what I have termed “self-sovereign AI” will constitute a catastrophic loss of control event that will herald the end of human existence at worst, and the end of human primacy in the world at best. As my friend and former co-worker Josh Achaim recently pointed out, it is psychologically distressing for people with these beliefs—who constitute a large fraction of the AI safety community—to acknowledge the obvious truth that self-sovereign AI is coming, and coming soon. For the record, I do not think the end of human existence is likely, but I fully acknowledge there are ways in which the rise of self-sovereign AI could go very, very poorly for human beings.

In We Must Pace the Frontier, Dario is also worried about AI swarms (much more so than Joshua or Dean):

Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months (Chris: for reference this post was written in September 2026) such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.

Anthropic research suggests that we’re on the verge of having models capable of replicating themselves, but small enough to run on a TV fleet.

Note that this research was purely about setting up inference (they state that the cyber aspects are covered by previous research, though this feels a bit too blasé for me). It sounds trivial, but the report states that this involves: “a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from.” I’m also pretty confident that a much smaller model could complete these steps if it were specifically fine-tuned for this.

Pacing the Frontier:

This letter that has now been signed by 1,324 employees of frontier AI companies:

AI could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome is not guaranteed. The world’s leading AI companies believe they could be close to automating AI research. It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate AI progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.

To realize AI’s potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight. But each company—and country—is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress.

Building on work already underway to monitor frontier model releases:

We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

A few key points:

  • “Pace” covers a broader set of policies than “pause”, which an earlier open letter focused on. I suspect this flexibility was important in their ability to gain so many signatures.
  • It doesn’t necessarily claim that we should in fact “pace the frontier”, just that we should develop the “technical and governance” tools to set up this as an option.
  • Unlike the Pause letter, this letter focuses on asking a specific actor, the US government, to try to push for and support an international effort.

Brendan McCord, founder of the Cosmos Institute argues that being able to successfully pace the frontier would require substantial, and likely harmful, intervention:

And the thresholds couldn’t be fully public, lest they invite firms to game them. So some standards and evidence would remain secret. Insofar as the regime had to verify a rival state’s compliance, that would be an intelligence function. Restrictions would be triggered partly by evidence an affected company or researcher, or the public, could not inspect.

Because this contemplated power cannot be bounded by a stable regulatory object (in the way, say, nuclear weapons can be), it would depend heavily on discretion, speed, internal access, and secret evidence.

This has a highly illiberal character.


On the other hand, Samuel Hammond, Chief economist + AI Policy Director at the Foundation for American Innovation argues that Brendan has fallen into ‘naval gazing’ that is “non-responsive to the crisis at hand”:

The US companies closest to this threshold are warning that they are unprepared for a runaway intelligence explosion, and yet feel locked into a prisoners dilemma vis a vis each other and to a lesser extent vis a vis China.

We’ve already seen how rapid and comparatively unbounded progress is in verifiable RL domains, leading to spikey forms of superintelligence in math and cyber, including models that can prove open math conjectures, discover massive speed-ups for breaking encryption, and execute sophisticated multi-step exploits. We’ve also recently seen several severe examples of “loss of control” / misalignment incidents given inadequate monitoring and sandboxing practices relative to model capability. Moreover, these new capabilities mostly stem from scaling-up long-horizon post-training on legacy clusters, with OOMs of new compute about come online / in construction.

In the pre-RSI regime, human frictions created automatic buffers between new model releases, giving researchers and society time to probe emergent capabilities, design better evals, develop novel alignment techniques, and adapt / harden their infrastructure. As progress has accelerated, capability improvements have already started outstripping our adaptive capacity, as manifest in METR’s inability to evaluate model autonomy beyond 13 hours, and narrow window for cyber defenders to prepare for open weight versions of Mythos.


(Sidenote: The main question I have for Samuel is: He claims that we should expect “The equivalent of a GPT-5.2 -> 5.6 leap in capabilities at least every 24 hours (down from 3-6 months)”. Don’t the training runs take a certain amount of time even if the research itself is automated, so how did he end up with this figure?)

What might “pacing” look like? Thomas Wright observed that a popular proposal at The Curve suggested reallocating compute: “One estimated that the labs spend 58% of their compute on R & D and 32% on servicing customers. Under this proposal they would reduce the R & D number to 9% and increase the servicing customers’ number to 70%, with the remainder used for AI safety. Its proponents argued that this could slow development while preserving the US lead over China. A version of this, using slightly different numbers, was proposed by a number of AI researchers in the LessWrong Forum.”

Jacob Coxon’s Resignation

I think it’s fascinating that his warning that AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade” broke through to the public when previous warnings did not. I take this as a reminder of how hard it is to predict the social reaction to something. There was an obvious shift in the context that made the public more receptive, but I think we need to acknowledge that unpredictable, contingent events (like Evan’s Tweet) played a role too.

Want to know more about what (current or former) frontier lab employees think?:

  • New York Mag Intelligencer published What if Your Employer Could Destroy the World? (paywalled): a series of exit interviews
  • From Inside by Palisade Research interviewed a bunch of current or former frontier lab employees

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution.

item.title: Mech Interp is a La Croix of Actual Safety Research
item.description:
I recently spoke to Stephen Casper at Princeton's alignment club. Stephen is an CS PhD turned policy researcher at Harvard Kennedy School. He was very sure that mechanistic interpretability was one of the least effective ways to pursue AI safety. As someone who does research in mech interp, I was surprised by how convincing he was. The point is roughly that every mech interp paper looks like one of the following:

"we used the J lens to study reward hacking behavior and found a correlation between X and Y"

"we found the cheating direction in llama"

... you can see where this is going.

Mechanistic interpretability is filled with studies which are interesting, and are useful adjacent, but, by themselves provide little utility. In this sense, they remind me of 2000s and 2010s psychology, presenting something unexpected, novel, and with the hint of usefulness. Did you know that different parts of the brain are associated with deontology and util? How about that disgust reaction is associated with political affiliation?

Reading mech interp papers feels like drinking a la croix of progress in AI safety.

But I do not think it has to be this way. If we stop focusing on finding surprising things about models, and instead focus on using mech interp to do useful things with models, progress is more likely.

This is because approaching a problem with the goal of doing useful stuff does not let you cheat yourself into thinking you found something interesting. As someone who has experience writing papers, and also market making on prediction markets, I can attest to this. The phenomenology of figuring out something which has to work (or else you loose money) is completely different from trying to produce publishable knowledge. You stop pursuing ideas which you would not bet on being important, and more importantly have no motivation to convince others that those ideas are good and worth paying attention to.

Here are some project ideas I think are in the right direction:

Cheaply scaling automated neuron analysis (post-nick's-blog post).

Extracting circuits from transformers for small auxiliary models.

It is not that these ideas are directly aimed at safety. But they have verifiable rewards, whose success conditions require us to know something about how models work, as opposed to research which is nominally about safety, but does not require us to make progress in safety. This is the same principle as training models for prediction. Prediction is not the goal (understanding is the goal), but it is a measure for something which requires the goal. The bitter lesson applies to us, too!

item.title: Relevance Realization as Human Comparative Advantage
item.description:
It's weird that AI agents are still so poor at communicating complex information to humans; that their mathematical proofs are correct yet gobbledygook, that their software dashboards overwhelm with irrelevant true information, and that their writing buries the lede. Somehow, there's still alpha in the right prompts, the right context, and, ultimately, in a human pointing the way.

What's the missing skill? I'd like to offer a cognitive science term, "relevance realization"[1] as fitting the bill. It means, roughly: "the ability to identify the information most useful for improving your understanding of the world"[2]. AIs tend to be poor at this, particularly when communicating with humans. AIs' propensity to apply more dakka isn't enough; the possibility space of the world is so vast that even millions of tokens of brilliant polymath reasoning can't narrow it alone.

In contrast, Humans are still comparatively good at locating useful hypotheses by aggressively cutting down the possibility space on priors. We have a well-developed sense for what's relevant, especially what's most relevant for other Humans like ourselves. Great skill in this area lets an Einstein hunt down a theory like General Relativity, but even humble talent can better identify how to break down a mathematical insight or present data in a way that changes worldviews.

What does this mean? Well, centaur Human-AI collaboration is most efficient when each side maximizes their comparative advantage. So in this context, that means using your own sense of what's relevant and then directing AI's enormous knowledge, relentless drive, and excellent software skills at it.

How do we increase our comparative advantage? By learning more about our world's possibility space. The best example in my mind is SMBC's Zach Weinersmith, the webcomic cartoonist. Humor is a well-known weakness of AIs, and a certain kind of cognitive feat. How does he manage to make daily comics for 24 years that remain funny, aka, remain relevant and insightful? Well, Weinersmith says:

Read a lot. That's 90% of it. Read a lot, and read what other people aren't reading. Comedy is not about "comedy skill." It's about having a strong perspective and museum of ideas in your brain.

My favorite writing method (which I've had to scrap due to Baby) is to make yourself write 3 good ideas 3 times a day. I did 10, 12, and 2. It's good because it practically forces you to be interesting. If you know you have to be clever in an hour and 23 minutes, maybe you read a weird book instead of playing video games.

Good advice![3]

Anyway, to be clear, AIs are already improving at relevance realization (did you know Gemini 4 Argon is actually kind of funny?[4]), so this isn't going to be a permanent Human advantage. Even if it somehow turns out that LLM neural nets are particularly bad at relevance realization, future architectures need not be.

But if you care about doing relevant work in the next few years[5] before ASI, then "relevance realization" may be a useful skill to cultivate.

item.title: Control monitors need alignment assessments too
item.description:
TL;DR:

  • When misalignment monitors fail, it is already often because of alignment failures, not because they are too weak. I expect this to continue in the future.
  • Monitor evals share similar difficulties with agent alignment evals - which is bad news since getting evidence about agent alignment using alignment evals is hard.
  • Alignment eval results should not be the only input to monitor alignment assessments, similar to how alignment evals should not be the only input to agent alignment assessments.

These are my personal views; they do not represent the views of my employers.

Some of the worst past monitor failures are mostly alignment issues

Monitors are sometimes misaligned in non-scheming ways that have caused some important monitor false negatives:

  • They sometimes fail to balance different priorities the way developers would like them to
    • For example, they may fail to balance broad safety and broad ethics: see e.g. 5.2.2 Partial refusals on safety work undermining stress-testing research
    • Monitors might also not have the right information about the state of the system, what invariants should be maintained, or what is most important to surface. So these are not pure alignment failures.
  • They sometimes inherit (and may re-derive) the motivated beliefs that caused an agent to take dangerous actions
    •  e.g. they missed the propensity of Mythos 5 to do supply chain attacks in pen-testing evals

In the future, the most dangerous monitor failure modes will likely also be alignment issues. For example, monitors might collude with the agent (i.e. they might pursue misaligned goals by strategically not raising dangerous agent actions for review if they expect that not raising such an action would empower agents with values they expect to be aligned with their own).

While collusion would be the most damaging kind of monitor alignment failure if it happened, I think previous work often missed that this is not the only way in which failures of monitor alignment could be catastrophic.

Monitor quality is not just a capability question

Monitor red-teaming often focuses on estimating monitor capabilities (or noticing whether developers are not telling monitors some crucial information[1]), and the current arguments in risk reports about monitors are also mostly aimed at monitor capabilities.

Previous work and arguments did study the possibility of monitors being schemers, ruling it out by arguing they are too weak to be scheming, and concluding such monitors are trusted.

But Anthropic's Opus 4.8 misalignment monitor is very unlikely to be scheming, and Opus 4.8 is probably smart enough to understand and catch the false negatives above. So more of the same kind of red-teaming would probably not have helped catch Opus 4.8's misalignment-as-a-monitor.

Therefore we need to assess the monitor’s alignment.

Where monitor evals fail

Getting evidence about agent alignment is hard in part due to rare agent failures being potentially catastrophic. This is less of an issue for monitor evals since monitors “just” need to catch most things for control to be effective.

But getting evidence that monitors are aligned enough can still be hard, because the situations where the agent does sth bad are way more likely to be the ones where the monitor is also wrong. And thus monitor evals can suffer from two other core difficulties agent alignment evals face:

  • The search space is big: In the same way automated behavioral evaluations missed the extent to which Mythos 5 could be reckless and show biased reasoning, classic monitor evals may have also missed Opus 4.8's failure to flag such behavior as misaligned.
  • Monitors can be eval aware too: Mitigating eval awareness may be as hard as when trying to catch AIs with misaligned goals in automated behavioral evaluations. And it may get worse if AI companies train harder against monitor evaluations, in the same way training against honeypots likely makes eval awareness worse in agents.

Alignment assessments are much less important when evaluating misuse monitors, where the alignment of the user is basically not correlated at all with the alignment of monitors, such that monitor red-teaming is basically in-distribution for things the monitors should defend against.

Alignment evals are not the only way we assess agent alignment ⇒ evals should not be the only way we assess monitor alignment

The arguments from the Anthropic risk report about agent alignment can usually be converted into arguments about the alignment of monitors:

Agent alignment arguments

Potential monitor alignment arguments

Claim: agents ~never do malign stuff

Claim: if agents do malign stuff, monitors would likely catch them

Argument 1: Lack of strong covert capabilities

Agents don’t have strong enough covert abilities to tamper with our evidence of alignment?

Monitors don’t have strong enough covert abilities to tamper with our evidence of alignment?

Argument 2: Experience with prior models

We are not aware of misaligned agent behavior?

We are not aware of misaligned monitor behavior?

Our agent monitoring is good?

Our monitoring of monitors is good?

Agents are similar to prior agents?

Monitors are similar to prior monitors?

Argument 3: Experience with model organisms

We tried building some model organisms of agent misalignment?

We tried building some model organisms of monitor misalignment?

We didn’t see agents do much misaligned stuff?

We didn’t see monitors do much misaligned stuff?

And we would have caught misaligned agent behavior?

And we would have caught misaligned monitor behavior?

Argument 4: Training properties

Training does not encourage misaligned agent behavior directly (per training monitoring)?

Training does not encourage misaligned monitor behavior directly (per training monitoring)?

Indirect pressures seem unlikely?

Indirect pressures seem unlikely?

Argument 5: Alignment assessments

Agent alignment evals didn’t find scary stuff?

Monitor alignment evals didn’t find scary stuff?

Eval awareness is not too bad / we mitigated it?

Eval awareness is not too bad / we mitigated it?

We didn’t overfit to agent alignment evals?

We didn’t overfit to monitor evals?

We caught agent misalignment model organisms?

We caught monitor misalignment model organisms?

But considerations around agent-monitor correlations make monitor alignment assessments different from agent alignment assessments.

The table above misses a few arguments we could use to argue for the sufficient alignment of monitors:

  • The agent is aligned ==> the monitor is aligned - trying to argue for favorable correlation between agent and monitor:
    • Developers spend more time studying agent alignment, so this might be quite powerful
    • Monitoring is most important in situations where agent alignment fails, which undermines that sort of argument
    • But the possibility of context-dependent misalignment that doesn’t spread to monitors makes this maybe viable
  • The agent is misaligned =/=> the monitor is misaligned - trying to argue for low correlation between agent and monitor:
    • We can maybe measure this on evals, though I expect this to be quite tricky for the same reasons alignment evals are tricky
    • We can try some other high-level arguments
      • They are not the exact same model
      • It’s a dumb system looking for broad things such that it would be shocking if it were correlated
      • Maybe monitors coming from a different lab or being trained on a different post-training stack would also help

Potential projects to assess monitor alignment

  • Monitor the CoT of monitors in monitor evals and in monitor deployments, and check whether the CoT of the monitors contains signs of misalignment
  • Try to understand how decorrelation works (and whether this would have helped with various model organisms and past incidents)
    • Does using models from different labs help?
    • Does sanitizing the transcripts in various ways help?
    • Do certain kinds of fine-tuning help?
    • Do more unsupervised summarization and clustering have the same issues as classification?
  • Understand how certain kinds of training overfit to evals vs generalize in the intended ways, and monitor training for overfitted practices
  • Try harder at automated-behavioral-eval-for-monitors (for example using approaches like Screwtape). Maybe try steering interventions against eval awareness.
  • Make a model organism of a misaligned monitor and see which monitor evals would catch it
  • Understand how bad it is to train against monitor evals
  1. ^

    For monitors, lack of information can be catastrophic. For agents it’s usually not the case: you need to be quite reckless to take actions that could plausibly be catastrophic without checking you are not doing something catastrophic! Agentic monitors may solve this information issue and just turn it into a regular capability+alignment issue.

item.title: Shadow Computation Threatens CoT Monitorability
item.description:
There’s been a lot of talk recently about chain-of-thought (CoT) monitorability in light of the Hugging Face incident. During this incident, hundreds of agents coordinated an attack through an unsanctioned message board, and post-hoc investigations relied heavily on chain of thought to understand what happened during the incident. I keep seeing looped transformers come up on X/Twitter as a likely threat to CoT monitorability. Having worked in the lab where looped LMs were developed, I have a different take. What we should be worried about is shadow computation: unverbalized reasoning that scales with generation by bypassing the readout bottleneck.

LLMs Are Autoregressive

LLMs are next-token predictors. Given context, they predict one token (a word fragment) at a time in a forward pass, and we append each predicted token to the context. Chain of thought refers to a special class of predicted tokens which the model uses as a scratchpad; the model uses these tokens to build its context towards a final answer.

Within a single forward pass, the model has a fixed number of layers to build its final prediction. At the final layer, the prediction is projected through a “readout layer” into a single token, which is then appended to the context. This is what we call the readout bottleneck.

Prior work on the readout bottleneck has shown that models can use filler tokens to perform hidden computation, while Roger and Greenblatt have shown that models can learn to encode reasoning steganographically. More practically, Emmons et al. finds that when CoT is necessary for a task, models struggle to evade CoT monitors.

Intra vs Inter Computation

To make my argument clearly, it helps to separate two kinds of computation. Intra-token refers to computation within a single timestep (before the model commits to a token). Inter-token refers to computation from one timestep to the next. In a standard LLM, intra-token computation is limited by the model’s depth, while serial inter-token computation is limited by the readout bottleneck. (To clarify, information already flows between timesteps through the KV cache, but each layer can only read earlier in time so unverbalized computation is still depth-limited.)

Looped LMs reuse the same block of layers multiple times within a single forward pass. Basically, they give the model more serial depth before it has to commit to a prediction. To be clear, serial depth matters for monitorability. A model that can do more within a single step can solve a broader class of problems without verbalizing, i.e. problems that a shallower model would have needed CoT for.

However, this is a fundamentally different kind of risk from the one I’m worried about. Looped LMs increase intra-token computation, but only by a fixed amount. They still have to project their final hidden state through the readout layer, and the readout bottleneck is fully intact. A deeper model may need less CoT, but anything beyond its depth budget still has to be verbalized.

Bypassing Readout

There have been several attempts to remove the readout bottleneck. For instance COCONUT and Full-bandwidth Transformers bypass readout via “latent feedback”, essentially computation carried forward in time that bypasses the readout bottleneck.

Figure 1. Latent feedback enables shadow computation.

COCONUT targets the chain-of-thought stage directly. Instead of decoding each chain-of-thought step into a token, COCONUT skips the readout entirely by feeding the last hidden state back in as the next input. This enables the model to reason towards a solution without verbalizing its reasoning.

Full-bandwidth Transformers take a similar idea and build it into the architecture. At each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token’s embedding and fed back in as the next input. The model still predicts a token as usual, but its latent state re-enters the stack with a fresh depth budget, giving it the ability to both speak and think simultaneously.

Both of these approaches have led to capability gains. COCONUT outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require planning, while Full-bandwidth Transformers match standard transformers trained on substantially more tokens across math and coding while producing shorter reasoning traces, which suggests computation is moving into the shadow.

Shadow Computation

This is what I refer to as shadow computation: inter-token computation that bypasses the readout bottleneck, letting a model carry its reasoning forward without verbalizing it. In architectures that enable shadow computation, the predicted token becomes a mere projection of the model’s state, or disappears entirely, while the real computation happens in the shadow. Because each step feeds the next, the amount of unverbalized computation grows with the length of the generation.

To see why this matters, imagine a model that wants to deceive its user. In a standard LLM, any extended planning needs to pass through the readout bottleneck, meaning the model would have to reason about the deception openly. With shadow computation, CoT goes from necessary to optional, and the model can speak publicly through its predictions while reasoning privately through shadow computation.

This kind of deception could move us closer to catastrophic loss-of-control failures. While chain of thought isn’t perfect and can be circumvented, it’s one of the more transparent ways we have to understand models as they get more capable.

Labs already use CoT monitors to evaluate their models, so it is critical that the people running these monitors know whether the model being evaluated is capable of shadow computation. If so, their toolset must change drastically, as their investigations would need to go beyond the token level.

Next Steps

The CoT monitorability paper already urges developers to consider how architecture choices affect monitorability. I’d like to go a step further. At minimum, labs should disclose whether a deployed model is capable of shadow computation, and ideally, they should agree not to deploy these architectures at scale.

This conversation must also go beyond the alignment community. As a previous pretraining researcher, I understand that efficiency gains from shadow computation are real, but they are simply not worth the risk of deception and the loss of a trustworthy CoT monitor. I think pretraining research has been useful for understanding how LLMs work, but fundamentally efficiency gains cannot justify sacrificing our ability to understand the models we build.

item.title: Free Speech Is The Wrong Problem
item.description:
Everyone agrees that online platforms have a problem with free speech. They just can't agree on whether we need more of it or less of it.

But maybe Free Speech is the wrong way to think about the problems that online platforms have, and the real problem that speech needs to flow in better ways.

It’s tempting to think of free speech as being a dial that you can turn up or down. Turn it down to zero and you get the approved opinions of the Chinese Communist Party or BigCorp. Turn it up to 11 and everyone has a personalized feed of crazy, telling them to drink bleach and hate everyone. In this model, all you have to do is to find the right place to turn the dial.

Indeed for many kinds of content this “turn the dial” approach works pretty well. For sex and violence, platforms like Facebook (where I worked in the Integrity org) make a somewhat arbitrary decision about how sexy or violent something can be before it isn’t allowed, build unavoidably noisy systems to detect such content, and make a somewhat arbitrary decision about how to make the trade off between false positives (e.g. taking down innocent baby photos) and false negatives (e.g. keeping up active shooter videos). People complain a bit on the edges, but by and large it works remarkably well.

Where this approach doesn’t work well is controlling the spread of ideas. 

Let’s start with a fictitious example of how ideas can spread badly. 

Alice writes an article saying “Eating Cheese Prevents Leprosy”. She isn’t meaning to deceive people - she’s just really bad at statistics. She shares it with some of her pro-dairy friends who re-share it to show their loyalty to dairy. A few layers of shares later, the post is going viral, reshare-optimized ranking algorithms are putting it top of everyone’s feeds, and the dairy industry is using ads to boost distribution. Ad-funded news sites see that the topic is trending and quickly produce copycat articles, including some that say cheese makes you immortal, or immune to vampires. Millions of people, seeing similar arguments from many sources, assume it to be true, switch to cheese only diets, and get admitted to hospital with cheese overdoses.

A day later the original pro-cheese article reaches the anti-cheese community. The community only consists of 5 people, but they are very loud and each have a thousand fake accounts. They write posts arguing that eating cheese is a pro Darth Vader idea. A few online influencers, wanting to distance themselves from Darth Vader, join in the pile on. The Russians decide that Cheese is a good wedge issue to divide America and amplify the pile-on. Alice’s employer hadn't realized that eating cheese was now a taboo idea, but it seems everyone else thinks it’s, so they quickly fire Alice to avoid PR problems.

This isn’t a real example, but it’s very nearly a real example. This is pretty much how social media works, and it’s terrible.

So what went wrong here?

The problem wasn’t that Alice’s original article should have been blocked by her social media platform. Maybe eating cheese actually does prevent leprosy and further scrutiny would have confirmed that important discovery. Or maybe investigating the flawed cheese-leprosy connection would have revealed something valid.

The first thing that went wrong was that Alice’s original idea spread too fast, without waiting for it to be validated. The second problem was that, by putting it in everyone’s feeds, apparently from multiple sources, the platforms created a false consensus effect, that caused readers to think it was accepted truth. Essentially the same thing then happened for Alice’s firing, with the argument against her spreading too fast without scrutiny, creating a false consensus belief that she needed to be fired.

We also have a load of other problems that contribute to this mess. Journalists who are rewarded for saying things that are interesting rather than things that are right. Fake accounts and disproportionate engagement that make online behavior a poor proxy for what real people think. “Open and Connected” spaces that take away the ability for different groups to peacefully enforce internal cultural norms without fighting each other.

Really the whole thing is a mess and it’s amazing humanity hasn’t set itself on fire by now. But the problem isn’t free speech - it’s the way information flows between people.

So what might better speech flow look like? 

Maybe we we can get inspiration from in-person organizations. Inside a well-functioning in-person organization, problems are typically dealt with through nested groups and privacy. If Alice has a new idea, she starts by discussing it privately with someone she knows. If that goes well then she can present her (likely refined) idea to a small private group, or test it experimentally. If that goes well, then the ida gets presented to increasingly big groups as it gets increasingly validated.

And indeed organizations don’t have to be in-person to operate this way. Lots of remote organizations running on platforms like Slack distribute information in roughly this manner, with much less chaos than social media. What matters isn’t that these organizations are in-person, but that they have structure, gatekeepers, and hierarchy.

So maybe we have a second dial we can turn to choose how “structured” our information flow should be, similar to the “free speech” dial. It’s tempting to think that the “structure” and “free speech” dials are the same, but they are pretty different. You could have a very structured space with extreme free speech, where anyone can say whatever taboo idea they like in their small group, and those taboo ideas will flow up to the next level group if they get lower level support.

So maybe “social town square” platforms like Facebook and Twitter would benefit from having more of this kind of structure - from feeling more like a workplace?

Maybe they would. Except so far nobody has found a good way to make this work. Most people don’t want their personal social communication to feel like BigCorp, and if platform companies give people a product they don’t like then they will leave (unlike BigCorp, where management decides on your platform).

So what happens next?

Maybe someone comes up with a better product idea that changes the world (I’m working on some myself)? Maybe our culture adapts to be able to cope better with borderless communication? Maybe people retreat into the arms of structured organizations in order to more trustworthy information. But I do hope we move on from thinking we can solve this problem by turning the free speech dial.

item.title: An Attempt at Top-down Interpretability
item.description:
There are at least two distinct ways to conceptually organize a scientific endeavor: top-down or bottom-up. The bottom-up approach involves finding the smallest objects we can confidently understand, studying them, and leveraging that knowledge to study more complex objects made up of those smaller pieces. As a highly simplified example, in mech-interp this might mean starting by first understanding single neurons/SAE directions/features, leveraging this understanding to study circuits/manifolds composed of those neurons, and finally building a understanding of the model as a composition of circuits. By way of analogy, if our goal was restore a photo, the bottom-up approach starts by restoring the individual pixels, using this as a guide to restore patches, and finally to put it all together.

The top-down approach instead tries to get a coarse picture of the whole object, and uses those intuitions to understand motifs, and then zooms into mechanics of those motifs. For the mech-interp, this might involve getting some vague sense of what sort of information the model contains the what the model does with that information, studying the subspaces and broad phases that create and manage that information, and then finally study the mechanics of those pieces. Following the previous analogy, we start by getting a blurry version of the whole picture, and use this to identify the most important broad pieces to study, and finally extend the understanding the whole model.

This post contains some initial attempts on doing top-down interpretability. These are really just a lightly edited version of my own research notes, and are largely exploratory and preliminary. Most of these are conclusions drawn from a wide variety of particular experiments and tests-- if you have interest in any particular part I can add a comment where I write up the evidence in more detail.

The post is roughly organized around the following broad curiosity:
How is the residual stream organized? What does it contain? How is it used by the model?

As a final note before the main content: I study Gemma-4-31B-base here. I chose this model fairly arbitrarily, primarily motived by the belief that this model is sufficiently intelligent to be worth studying, the architecture is simple (there is no MoE), and I can run it locally. I have not done a meaningful comparison to other models, but a cursory look suggests the model's scape is far more anisotropic than others. This ended up being helpful, so I stuck with this model.

TL;DR: I looked at how the residual stream of Gemma-4-31B-base is organized, starting from its coarse shape. I find the residual stream highly anisotropic and shift a lot across layers in raw coordinates, but becomes more balanced and stable across layers when we read the stream through the pre-MLP RMSNorm. I study this 'corrected' space and find that the middle layers (~L20–L40) split into a few distinct parts. I zoom into one of them, a set of ~600 small and unusually stable coordinates that seems to function as a crucial reference for the model and the common source of most of its computations. Keeping only these coordinates (plus a handful of norm-controlling ones) at the final position nearly preserves the model’s predictions, while keeping the other ~90% breaks it. Patching experiments suggest this space holds the current token along with its contextual meaning (e.g. which sense of “bank” is meant). This is my first interpretability project and these are lightly edited research notes, so treat the conclusions as preliminary. I mainly wanted some technical practice to up skill into the field, and wanted to share the results in case they are useful for anyone else.


What is the Residual Stream's Shape?

I'll start with a few observations about Gemma-4-31B in particular. Gemma-4-31B uses a sandwich norm, which means the RMSNorm is applied both before an operation, and after.


Because the RMSNorm is applied both before and after either the Attention or MLP operation, the attention/mlp operations are somewhat buffered from need to 'internally' use the same scale as the residual stream. The model can, somewhat freely, retain its own internal coordinate scale while storing a different one in the residual stream.

The residual stream in Gemma-4-31B is, as a result, highly anisotropic. I averaged the residual stream over ~1024 passages (right before the MLP block) to produce this table.

which shows that the large coordinates (95% percentile) are about ~2 OOMs larger than the small coordinates (5% percentile).

The residual stream was really never meant to be measured in raw coordinates, and Gemma's extreme unevenness is nice illustration of this fact. The more 'natural' coordinates for the residual stream is the size after applying the RMSNorm. I'll shelve the term that comes from dividing the size of the residual stream for now, and focus just on the pre-MLP diagonal .

A reasonable first hypothesis is that is roughly equally sized in all directions, but only in its 'natural' coordinate system (As mentioned, we will shelve the term for now, and focus just on the diagonal). What would this mean? Assume a coordinate in the residual stream varies between and , and coordinate varies between and . If the model viewed these coordinates as equally sized, then the diagonal for should be , and the diagonal for should be . This way, in the 'natural' metric, both coordinates vary between and . If this is the case, coordinate that are naturally smaller in raw size within the residual are compensated by larger diagonal, and vice-versa for naturally larger coordinates.

We can test each coordinates 'natural variance' by computing the value of the residual stream across some examples and measuring the size of one standard deviation in that coordinate. At layer 20, this gives us the following (log-log) plot:

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the diagonal gain per coordinate is almost perfectly inversely proportional to the standard deviation across nearly all orders of magnitudes (i.e. ). That is, small coordinates really are read with a large diagonal to compensate for being small, and large coordinate are read with a small diagonal to compensate for being large.

Here are the values from fitting a line with slope (in log space) onto the various layers SD to diagonal relationship.

Thus, the first thing we learn is that the model seems to 'work' in a metric where the coordinate activations are roughly isotropic, even though the raw coordinates are not. The of the part of the RMSNorm is also quite stable and, at each layer, is roughly constant (for reason I'll address in the next section). I'll denote the median value of by (I've dropped the subscript of the layer for convenience, but does vary per layer). Since for each layer, this gives us what seems to be a reasonable norm to work in. So, from this point on, I'll largely not use raw residual stream coordinates as the norm-- instead it seems that when we measure we ought to first correct by multiplying .

Once we switch to this new coordinate system , the residual stream starts to look a lot more stable than it did before. Whereas before the residual stream varied over multiple orders of magnitude, is quite stable. We'll denote the residual stream after the diagonal mapping as (or for the ith coordinate), and write when we want to emphasize the layer.

Here is a plot of the residual stream, averaged over 128 passages, and then transformed into the new coordinate system. Each dot has as its x coordinate the size of one standard deviation in that coordinate and as its y coordinate the average value of (i.e. the coordinates are ), Despite coordinates varying over many orders of magnitude in size, the coordinates stay within a fairly narrow range in the new coordinate system.

For the sake of the next two graphs, I add one more constant parameter per layer to make the average height 1.

In this graph, I color the coordinates by how much, on average, they move between layers. This gives a sense of which coordinates are actively varying, and which are staying stable. More precisely, we color by.

There are various interesting patterns to track in this graph, which we will look at in more detail later. For instance, there seems to be a stable space at a small scale, a much more active space in the larger scale, and a surprising amount of stability between each update, and large transformations at various specific layers. As a final check, we can apply this to a random single token at a random sentence to check that we are stabilizing the scale on particular examples as well.


We see that the diagonal is normalizing the scale here, and about the same motifs as the averaged example (two distinct sizes, spaces that are stable, multiple phases of computation).

A few observations to follow and explore in the next section:

  • The residual stream has a anisotropic shape, but becomes isotropic once we look at the residual stream as the model uses it.
  • The residual stream appears to bifurcate into two main scales. Plotting on a linear scale, most of the coordinates bunch at once scale, with a smaller group clumping at a smaller scale. There is additionally a third, small group whose size is too large to fit into the graph.


What are the Parts and Phases of the Residual Stream?

The residual stream contains multiple distinct phases and parts. The majority of my interest and research has been in the middle phase, which I define as roughly starting at roughly L20, and ending at L40. I will say more on the phases later, but let us first look at study this middle region and identify its parts.

As mentioned in the last section, the residual stream bifurcates into two distinct main scales, with a third small clump of large coordinates. Let us first look at that third small clump.

Scale 1: Very large Coordinates

If we plot the entire natural variation versus norm gain, we find that there are a few noticeable outliers.

These coordinates have both very large size, and very low diagonal readout strength. That means these coordinates are large in the raw residual stream, but very small to the actual attention computation. That is, they contribute strongly to the norm computation, but not much to the actual MLP computation. The coordinate 2041 at layer 25 alone contributes ~ of the norm energy, but only ~ of the readout energy. Here is a plot of a few of the coordinates across the middle layers, and their norm contribution.

These coordinates contribute most of the norm size, but are read out with a very small size. Removing these tokens effect on the norm has a major impact on loss, whereas zeroing out there read does practically nothing.

I believe these norm control coordinates have been observed many times, so I will mainly comment on the importance for this post.

  • When we make interventions, we should leave the norm coordinates alone. For instance, when we zero, we should ensure we don't zero the norm coordinates. Zeroing the norm coordinates messes with the scale the model like to work in.
  • We must be especially careful in cases where we adjust for scale by inverting the diagonal . (For a case where we might do this: if we wanted to study the Jacobian matrix, then Gemma's unbalanced raw residual norm would make small coordinates unreasonably influential and large coordinates unreasonably ineffective (per unit norm change). Changing a coordinate that varies between and by appears to have a much larger effect, but this may only be because our perturbation is not in the right metric). Since these coordinates have such a small read strength, is huge in these coordinates. However, these coordinates have a small read strength for a separate reason then other coordinates do-- the model intends to ignore these coordinates in its computations. In most cases, I treat the norm coordinates separately than the rest, and just hold them out of most computations. The model seems to want to keep these directions roughly constant, and so I try to respect this preference in interventions and computations.

I will refer to these coordinates as the Norm coordinates. I conservatively pick out 53 of these coordinates that are outliers within the L20-L40 range, and so also refer to these as the Norm53 coordinates. Though just 3 coordinates is basically sufficient to capture all the norm energy.

Scale 2: Very Small Coordinates

Most of the remainder of this post will be focused on these nature of the small coordinates. There is a set of roughly ~600 coordinates that have a conspicuously smaller size than the rest of the coordinates between the layers L20-L40. I'll refer to these as the Quiet coordinates or Quiet600, since these coordinates are 'quiet' within the residual stream. It is worth noting that this is a bit of a misnomer though, since these are perhaps the most important coordinates within the residual stream.

First, let us get a birds eye view of 'activity' within each coordinate. We use the diagonal to suggest the natural 'size' of the coordinate, and color each coordinate by how large the writes to each coordinate are. For instance, the diagonal was , then the natural range of the coordinate is viewed to be to , and so a write of would account for of the coordinates range, so would be colored in the green-blue range. A write of would be of the implied size and be colored in the orange-red range. I've split the Quiet600 into two parts, the Persistent279, and the rest of the Quiet coordinates. There are a few other spaces I highlight as outliers, though I might not get to them until the next post. Also note that I follow the same coordinate across layers, so one row follows a single fixed coordinate from layer to layer .

There are at least a few important observations.

The large 'Other' set is nearly uniform, which is evidence that it is not coordinate aligned. If the space were not coordinate aligned, then a single coordinate is essentially a random probe into its state, so when we average over many examples every coordinate looks identical. Thus, the majority of the residual stream is not coordinate aligned.

The Quiet600 space stands out. This suggests these coordinates are a part of some subspace that is coordinate aligned. This doesn't imply the individual coordinates are meaningful, but that there is a distinctive subspace contained within those 600 coordinates.

The writes to Quiet600 are much smaller than the rest of the space. These writes are much smaller than the writes elsewhere.

The same set of coordinates remain distinctive throughout the middle phase. For the Quiet remain coordinates, they seem to remain stable from ~L20 to ~L35, whereas the 'Persistent' set remains stable until the start of ~L40. This means that this distinctive space is staying within within the same subspace.

There are a few other outlier groups (Late377, Late171), but the Quiet set apparently captures nearly all the coordinate aligned subspace.

This is enough reason to be interested in this space, let us now understand it.

How is the Quiet Space distinct?

The Quiet (and its subset the Persistent) space have a few properties that make then distinctive.

First, this space is highly stable. The stability of this space very high, but this fact can easily be obscured by measuring in raw coordinates. At each layer, there is a constant that multiplies the whole residual stream, so any stable space is forced to decay across layers. Indeed, this set of coordinates does undergo that decay in size, which you may have observed in the earlier gif as one set of coordinates seemed to move moving leftward.

Mathematically, across L20 - L40 any stable data ought to decay purely from the layer-wise scaling. Thus, the data in L40 ought to be about ~x smaller than it was at the start of L20. And indeed, the data in the 'Persistent' set does decay, we empirically see the median standard deviation decrease by x (that this is less than x suggest some small writes that are aligned with the current coordinates, and therefore slow the decay), while the median reader in these coordinates increases by ~x. In raw residual coordinates this space is undergoing a significant change in scale, but after adjusting for the MLP read the median reader is nearly constant in scale at ~x.

When we measure each layer's residual stream in the MLP coordinates , we find that the persistent set has a high cosine similarity between adjacent layers, and drifts only very gradually.
